content: Asthma continues to be a major cause of preventable illness and death. Regular consultations with healthcare professionals are critical for monitoring symptoms and adjusting medications appropriately. Globally, healthcare systems are exploring the use of telephone and internet-based technologies to manage the increasing number of individuals with asthma and other chronic conditions. These remote methods may help improve health outcomes while reducing the strain on emergency and inpatient services. Remote check-ups could provide a discreet and efficient way to maintain contact with patients, but it remains unclear whether they are as effective as traditional face-to-face consultations or if they might lead to unforeseen negative consequences. The objective of this study was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of conducting asthma check-ups remotely compared to the standard face-to-face consultations. To achieve this, researchers identified relevant trials from the Cochrane Airways Review Group Specialised Register up to November 24, 2015. Additional searches were conducted on clinical trial registries, including www.clinicaltrials.gov and the World Health Organization (WHO) trials portal. Reference lists of other reviews were also examined, and trial authors were contacted for further information. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults or children with asthma. These trials compared remote check-ups conducted via any form of technology with standard face-to-face consultations. Studies that relied solely on automated telehealth interventions without personalized contact with a healthcare professional were excluded. Both published and unpublished data, as well as abstracts, were considered. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted numerical data. Disagreements were resolved through consensus, and study authors were contacted for missing information. Data were analyzed using odds ratios (ORs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences for continuous outcomes, employing random-effects models. The quality of evidence for all outcomes was assessed using the GRADE approach. Six studies, involving a total of 2,100 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Four studies, comprising 792 participants, were pooled for the main efficacy analyses. Additionally, a cluster implementation study with 1,213 participants and a study on oral steroid tapering in 95 participants were analyzed separately. The baseline asthma severity of participants varied across studies, but most studies included individuals with asthma who were on regular medications and excluded those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or severe asthma. One study specifically examined oral steroid tapering in severe refractory asthma, which was treated as a separate question. Blinding was not possible in these studies, and four out of six studies had high dropout rates, which may have introduced bias. The evidence was inconclusive regarding whether remote check-ups led to a higher need for oral corticosteroids during asthma exacerbations compared to face-to-face consultations. The confidence intervals (CIs) were wide (OR 1.74, 95% CI 0.41 to 7.44; 278 participants; low-quality evidence). In the face-to-face group, 21 out of 1,000 participants experienced exacerbations requiring oral steroids over three months, compared to 36 out of 1,000 (95% CI 9 to 139) in the remote check-up group. Exacerbations requiring treatment in the emergency department, hospital admission, or unscheduled healthcare visits were too infrequent to determine whether remote check-ups are a safe alternative to face-to-face consultations. Serious adverse events were not reported separately from exacerbation outcomes. There was no significant difference in asthma control, as measured by the Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ), or in quality of life, as assessed by the Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire (AQLQ), between remote and face-to-face check-ups. While significant harm from remote check-ups could be ruled out for these outcomes, the lack of blinding made the results less reliable. A larger implementation study comparing two general practice populations found that offering telephone check-ups and proactively contacting participants increased the number of individuals with asthma who received a review. However, it remains unclear whether these additional participants experienced improved asthma outcomes as a result of the telephone check-ups. In conclusion, current randomized evidence does not show any significant differences between face-to-face and remote asthma check-ups in terms of exacerbations, asthma control, or quality of life. However, there is insufficient data to definitively rule out differences in efficacy or to confirm whether remote asthma check-ups are a safe alternative to face-to-face consultations.
